title: 2 Corinthians 11:22–33
context: Paul’s fool’s speech reaches its surprising content. He matches his rivals’ Jewish credentials, then claims to be a better servant of Christ by listing not triumphs but sufferings: beatings, shipwrecks, dangers, sleeplessness, hunger, and daily anxiety for the churches. He chooses to boast of weakness, sealing the list with the humiliating escape from Damascus in a basket. Arminian and Reformed readers share the reading: apostolic authority is marked by the shape of the cross.

verses.text: Are they Hebrews? So am I. Are they Israelites? So am I. Are they the offspring of Abraham? So am I.
verses.arminianNotes: Are they Hebrews, Israelites, offspring of Abraham? So is he. Arminian and Reformed readers agree the rivals stressed Jewish credentials, which Paul shares fully.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that Paul does not despise his heritage, but refuses to make it the ground of authority (compare Philippians 3:4 to 8).

verses.text: Are they servants of Christ? (I speak as one beside himself.) I am more so: in labors more abundantly, in prisons more abundantly, in stripes above measure, and in deaths often.
verses.arminianNotes: Are they servants of Christ? He is more, in labors, prisons, beatings, and near deaths. Arminian and Reformed readers agree he redefines service by suffering, speaking as one beside himself.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the cross shaping true ministry: the servant is not above the master.

verses.text: Five times I received forty stripes minus one from the Jews.
verses.arminianNotes: Five times he received forty lashes minus one from Jewish authorities. Arminian and Reformed readers agree this reflects synagogue discipline (Deut 25:3) that Paul accepted while still seeking his people.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note his continued love for Israel despite persecution.

verses.text: Three times I was beaten with rods. Once I was stoned. Three times I suffered shipwreck. I have been a night and a day in the deep.
verses.arminianNotes: Three times beaten with rods, once stoned, three times shipwrecked, a night and day adrift. Arminian and Reformed readers agree Acts records only some of these events, so the list fills out his story.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see God’s preservation of his servant through repeated danger.

verses.text: I have been in travels often, perils of rivers, perils of robbers, perils from my countrymen, perils from the Gentiles, perils in the city, perils in the wilderness, perils in the sea, perils among false brothers;
verses.arminianNotes: Frequent journeys, dangers from rivers, robbers, his own people, Gentiles, city, wilderness, sea, and false brothers. Arminian and Reformed readers agree that the final item is the most painful: betrayal within the church.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that no realm of life was safe, yet he persevered in his calling.

verses.text: in labor and travail, in watchings often, in hunger and thirst, in fastings often, and in cold and nakedness.
verses.arminianNotes: Labor, hardship, sleepless nights, hunger, thirst, fasting, cold, and nakedness. Arminian and Reformed readers agree these are the costs of mission, not ascetic achievements.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see Paul identifying with Christ who had nowhere to lay his head.

verses.text: Besides those things that are outside, there is that which presses on me daily: anxiety for all the assemblies.
verses.arminianNotes: Beyond these is the daily pressure of anxiety for all the churches. Arminian and Reformed readers agree that pastoral care can be the heaviest burden.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that Paul’s concern is not distrust of God but love for the churches.

verses.text: Who is weak, and I am not weak? Who is caused to stumble, and I don’t burn with indignation?
verses.arminianNotes: Who is weak and he is not weak? Who stumbles and he does not burn? Arminian and Reformed readers agree this shows deep empathy and protective zeal.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see a shepherd who shares his people’s burdens.

verses.text: If I must boast, I will boast of the things that concern my weakness.
verses.arminianNotes: If he must boast, he will boast of his weakness. Arminian and Reformed readers agree this is the key to the whole speech.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see God’s strength displayed through weakness (12:9).

verses.text: The God and Father of the Lord Jesus Christ, he who is blessed forever more, knows that I don’t lie.
verses.arminianNotes: God, the Father of the Lord Jesus, knows he is not lying. Arminian and Reformed readers agree this solemn oath underscores the truth of a surprising list.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note Paul’s appeal to God’s knowledge as final witness.

verses.text: In Damascus the governor under King Aretas guarded the Damascenes’ city, desiring to arrest me.
verses.arminianNotes: In Damascus the governor under King Aretas guarded the city to seize him. Arminian and Reformed readers agree this is a historical event (compare Acts 9:23 to 25), though Acts emphasizes Jewish plotters.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the precise political arrangement in Damascus is debated by historians.

verses.text: I was let down in a basket through a window by the wall, and escaped his hands.
verses.arminianNotes: He was lowered in a basket through a window in the wall and escaped. Arminian and Reformed readers agree the humiliating escape is a deliberate anticlimax: his first story is of flight, not triumph.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see it as the opposite of a Roman soldier’s honor for being first over the wall, a reading many interpreters suggest, though it is not certain.
